1-1.text: Part one. Spotting the rule. ... A sequence is a list of numbers that follows a rule. Each number in it is called a term.

1-2.text: Look at the jumps: 4, 9, 14, 19 goes up by 5 each time. The term-to-term rule is "add 5".

1-3.text: So the next term is 19 plus 5, which is 24.

1-4.text: Sequences can go down too. 50, 44, 38, 32 goes down by 6 each time, so the next term is 32 minus 6, which is 26.

2-1.text: Part two. Multiplying rules. ... Some rules multiply. In 3, 6, 12, 24 each term is double the one before. The rule is "multiply by 2".

2-2.text: The gaps are 3, 6 and 12. They are not all the same, so the rule is not "add a number".

2-3.text: 2, 6, 18, 54 has the rule multiply by 3. The next terms are 54 times 3, which is 162, then 162 times 3, which is 486.

3-1.text: Part three. Special sequences. ... Square numbers: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25. They make squares of dots: 1 times 1, 2 times 2, 3 times 3, and so on.

3-2.text: Triangle numbers: 1, 3, 6, 10, 15. Each new row has one more dot, so the gaps grow: 2, 3, 4, 5.

3-3.text: The Fibonacci sequence: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8. Each term is the two before it added together, so the next one is 5 plus 8, which is 13.

4-1.text: Part four. Growing patterns. ... Here is a growing pattern. Pattern 1 has 3 squares, Pattern 2 has 5 and Pattern 3 has 7.

4-2.text: Each new pattern adds 2 squares: one on each arm.

4-3.text: For Pattern 10, start with 3 and add 2 nine more times: 3 plus 9 times 2, which is 3 plus 18, which is 21.

4-4.text: The rule for Pattern n is 2 n plus 1: n squares on each arm, plus the corner. Pattern 10: 2 times 10, plus 1, equals 21.

5-1.text: Part five. The nth term. ... The nth term is a rule that gives any term from its position, n. For 3 n plus 1, the 1st term is 3 times 1, plus 1, which is 4. Then come 7 and 10.

5-2.text: The 10th term is 3 times 10, plus 1, which is 31. No need to write out all ten terms!

5-3.text: Finding the rule: 5, 8, 11, 14 goes up by 3, so compare it with 3 n: 3, 6, 9, 12. Every term is 2 more, so the nth term is 3 n plus 2.

5-4.text: 10, 8, 6, 4 goes down by 2, so compare it with negative 2 n: negative 2, negative 4, negative 6, negative 8. Every term is 12 more, so the nth term is 12 minus 2 n.

5-5.text: Is 50 a term of 4 n plus 1? Try 4 n plus 1 equals 50. Then 4 n equals 49, and n equals 12 point 2 5. That is not a whole number, so no, 50 is not a term.
